It worked for the movie, and wow, does it work on Broadway, a double jolt of adrenaline and sugar to inspire the most helicoptered of tots to play hooky and go shred an ax.

cn.t: Lloyd Webber's energetic adaptation delights with talented kid performers who actually rock, though critics find the score uneven and the book workmanlike. Brightman earns praise, but the children steal the show.

sg.ra: With a 44'10" proscenium and a stage wider than most Broadway houses, Orchestra Center C-G is the only zone where you get the full picture head-on without sacrificing actor-face detail. Spectacle-heavy productions here (BTTF's DeLorean, Mamma Mia! dance numbers) are blocked edge-to-edge, so off-center seats lose pieces even a few rows in.

This is the house's quiet value zone: full center alignment matters more here than proximity does because the auditorium is wider than deep, so row V center still reads front-on. Last orchestra row is short (~6 seats) with unusual legroom per multiple patrons. Tradeoff specific to Winter Garden: the mezzanine overhang starts around row O per published guides, clipping the top of the stage — fine for naturalistic plays, worse for musicals with fly-in sets.

Wide-house penalty hits hardest here: because the auditorium is broader than deep, side-orchestra angles into the stage are sharper than in a typical Broadway house — the further out you sit, the more the upstage far corner disappears. Multiple patrons specifically call out stage-right pillars clipping their view on Salesman; works better for plays where action holds center than for musicals with full-stage choreography.

In a wider-than-deep house the front center mezzanine rescues the seat selection by giving you the one thing center orchestra can't: altitude to take in the full 44'10" proscenium at once. Multiple patrons specifically cite this row range for Mamma Mia! and BTTF over the rear orchestra, and it avoids both the pillar risk on the sides and the mezz overhang clipping rear stalls.

Wide-house geometry pushes the far-left and far-right mezz off at a sharp angle — the stage-opposite corner is the consistent casualty. Reviewers note the speaker stacks on the edge as a recurring blocker, and because the mezz is only ~9 rows deep, distance isn't the killer — angle is. Good option if you're watching a show where the action centers; poor for full-stage choreography.

sg.n: Box Seats (Box B, C, F, G)
sg.ra: The Winter Garden boxes are widely flagged as among the most obstructed in Broadway — the box structure itself blocks significant stage area and the side angle compounds it. Skip at any price.
